messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leo is a 55-year-old fashion designer, recently divorced, who sought therapy after a colleague accidentally brushed his shoulder in a fitting room and he reacted by shoving her away, hard. He sat in the first session with his arms crossed, his jaw tight, and said he had come because he was afraid of what he might do next.

The event that shaped him was not recent. It was a childhood lived in a house where his father’s moods dictated the temperature of every room. When his father was silent—standing in the kitchen doorway, not speaking, just looking—Leo learned to freeze. That kind of silence was never empty. It meant something dangerous was about to happen. The blow would follow, sometimes with an open hand, sometimes with a belt, sometimes with whatever was nearest. Leo cannot tell a clear story of any one beating, even to himself. The memories are fragmented: the sound of a buckle hitting linoleum, the sight of his own small hands gripping the edge of the sofa, the smell of his father’s beer breath. He has never been able to arrange these pieces into a coherent narrative. Sometimes, when he tries to remember, he feels nothing at all—just a flat, hollow numbness, as if the boy in those memories is a stranger. But other times, the guilt hits him without warning. He dwells on what he did wrong, replaying moments before the beatings, searching for the mistake he must have made. He knows, intellectually, that a child does not cause a parent’s violence. But the feeling does not listen to intellect.

As an adult, Leo built a career in fashion, a world of precise touch and close physical proximity. He became known for his meticulous hand-finishing, for the way he could adjust a seam on a model without a word. But in the last few years, that world has become treacherous. He reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly—a tailor tapping his shoulder, a client reaching for his arm. He has learned to position himself with his back to the wall in every workroom. At home, he remains on guard. Even in his own apartment, he cannot fully relax. He scans rooms when he enters, checks behind doors, feels a tightness in his chest that never fully releases. He has come to believe that he is permanently changed for the worse, that the damage is inside him now, structural, like a garment that has been cut wrong and cannot be unpicked.

He avoids sleep. He knows that certain times of day—particularly the late evening, when the light goes gray and the house grows quiet—tend to bring on nightmares. So he stays up, sketching, drinking coffee, until exhaustion overrides vigilance. His divorce, two years ago, was partly a casualty of this. His wife could not understand why he would flinch when she touched him in bed, why he would sometimes get up and leave the room in the middle of the night, why he seemed to be waiting for something bad to happen even when nothing was wrong. He could not explain it to her. He could barely explain it to himself.

What finally brought him to therapy was the incident in the fitting room. The colleague was a young woman he had mentored for years. She was not a threat. He knew she was not a threat. But the feeling came before the thought—his arm shot out, and she stumbled back into a rack of garments. He saw her face, shocked and hurt, and he heard himself apologizing over and over. That night, he sat alone in his apartment and thought: I am going crazy. My reactions mean I am losing my mind. He had always told himself that he could manage, that the past was the past, that his vigilance was just caution. But now he was a danger to the people around him. And he could not stand the thought of becoming the thing he had spent his whole life trying not to be.
